\chapter{Easy, Hard, Tall}
\label{ch:mr-easy-hard-tall}
\hlchaptermodality{52}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say a thing is easy or difficult and a person is tall, and I can sort every adjective I own into the two classes by looking at its last letter.}

Complete MR-R52-easy-hard-tall and describe a person in three sentences -- tall, clever, a good friend -- which is the shape the A1 speaking paper's one-minute description asks for.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sopā]{\mr{सोपा} (sopā) — easy}

\label{lesson:MR-C52-sopa}



\begin{quote}
Six adjectives in, and only two of them agree. Here is a third that does, so the ending muscle does not go cold.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hushār}, then \emph{kharāb}, and name the class they share
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{सोपा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{सोपा}} — \emph{sopā} — \textbf{easy, simple}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{सोपा} · \mr{सोपी} · \mr{सोपं}} — \emph{sopā · sopī · sopaṁ}
\end{quote}

It ends in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}, so all three forms are yours already. The third adjective to behave this way and the first that costs nothing to conjugate, which is the point of having had the rule named in chapter forty-nine.

The sentence to keep is the one about the language itself:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मराठी} \mr{सोपी} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{marāṭhī sopī āhe.} — \textbf{Marathi is easy.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{मराठी}} is feminine, so the adjective ends in \textbf{-\mr{ी}}. Say it out loud; you have earned it, and it is true more often than a beginner expects.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sopā · sopī · sopaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{marāṭhī sopī āhe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} join two judgements with \textbf{\mr{आणि}} — \emph{lahān āṇi sopī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What gender is \textbf{\mr{मराठी}}, and what does \textbf{\mr{सोपा}} become with it? (\textbf{Feminine}; \textbf{\mr{सोपी}}.) Which class does \textbf{\mr{सोपा}} belong to? (\textbf{The agreeing one}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{सोपा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kaṭhīṇ]{\mr{कठीण} (kaṭhīṇ) — hard, difficult}

\label{lesson:MR-C52-kathin}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{सोपा}} without its opposite is an opinion nobody can disagree with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{कठीण}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{कठीण}} — \emph{kaṭhīṇ} — \textbf{hard, difficult}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मराठी} \mr{कठीण} \mr{नाही}.} — \emph{marāṭhī kaṭhīṇ nāhī.} — \textbf{Marathi is not difficult.}
\end{quote}

No ending, in any gender: the last letter is not \textbf{-\mr{आ}}, so the class is settled before you look anything up. Its opposite \textbf{\mr{सोपा}} agrees and it does not, which is a useful pair to hold precisely because the two halves behave differently.

Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कठिन}} (\emph{kaṭhina}) meant \textbf{hard} in the physical sense — a hard stone, hard ground. Marathi kept the word and moved it almost entirely onto tasks: \textbf{\mr{कठीण} \mr{काम}}, hard work; \textbf{\mr{कठीण} \mr{भाषा}}, a hard language. For a hard OBJECT a Marathi speaker will normally reach for another word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kaṭhīṇ} — hard, difficult
  \item \emph{marāṭhī kaṭhīṇ nāhī}
  \item \emph{sopī kiṁvā kaṭhīṇ?} — and hear only one of the two move
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{\mr{कठिन}} mean in Sanskrit? (\textbf{Physically hard}.) Does \textbf{\mr{कठीण}} agree? (\textbf{No}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%A0\%E0\%A5\%80\%E0\%A4\%A3}{Wiktionary: \mr{कठीण}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uṁch]{\mr{उंच} (uṁch) — tall, high}

\label{lesson:MR-C52-unch}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मोठा}} and \textbf{\mr{लहान}} measure a thing in every direction at once. A person has one direction that matters more than the others.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{उंच}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{उंच}} — \emph{uṁch} — \textbf{tall, high}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माझा} \mr{मित्र} \mr{उंच} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{mājhā mitra uṁch āhe.} — \textbf{my friend is tall.}
\end{quote}

Invariable, like most of what you have met: no \textbf{-\mr{आ}}, no ending. It works on a person, a building and a hill without changing, and it is the natural partner of the \textbf{\mr{वर}} you learned in chapter forty-two — what is \textbf{\mr{उंच}} is what is high \textbf{\mr{वर}}.

The pair to hold is \textbf{\mr{उंच}} against \textbf{\mr{मोठा}}. A \textbf{\mr{मोठा} \mr{मित्र}} is a big or an elder friend; an \textbf{\mr{उंच} \mr{मित्र}} is a tall one. English \emph{big} blurs the two and Marathi keeps them apart, which matters the moment somebody asks you to describe a person for a minute.

Its ancestor is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{उच्च}} (\emph{ucca}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{high, lofty}\textquotedblright{} — the same syllable that sits inside words for height across the Indo-Aryan languages.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{uṁch} — tall
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhā mitra uṁch āhe}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{uṁch} and \emph{moṭhā} back to back, and name the difference
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mitrālā} and describe the friend you can now see
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word would you use for a \textbf{tall} friend, and which for a \textbf{big} one? (\textbf{\mr{उंच}}; \textbf{\mr{मोठा}}.) Does \textbf{\mr{उंच}} agree? (\textbf{No}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%89\%E0\%A4\%82\%E0\%A4\%9A}{Wiktionary: \mr{उंच}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sopā · kaṭhīṇ · uṁch]{Describe a person for the first time}

\label{lesson:MR-R52-easy-hard-tall}



\begin{quote}
Nine adjectives are now yours. Sort all nine into the two classes before you use any of them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three that agree — \emph{\textbf{\mr{मोठा}}}, \emph{\textbf{\mr{चांगला}}}, \emph{\textbf{\mr{सोपा}}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the ones that never do — \emph{\textbf{\mr{लहान}}}, \emph{\textbf{\mr{सुंदर}}}, \emph{\textbf{\mr{खराब}}}, \emph{\textbf{\mr{हुशार}}}, \emph{\textbf{\mr{कठीण}}}, \emph{\textbf{\mr{उंच}}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhā mitra uṁch āhe paṇ lahān nāhī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chāṅglā mitra} — with the adjective in front, where it belongs
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mī mitrālā pāṇī deto} and then judge the water
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You can now describe a house, a room, a language and a person. Which single test decides whether an adjective takes an ending? (\textbf{Does it end in -\mr{आ}?}) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
